related-article.article-title: Effects of spatial constraints of inhibitory connectivity on the dynamical development of criticality in spiking networks.
Effects of spatial constraints of inhibitory connectivity on the dynamical development of criticality in spiking networks.

abstract.p: Neural systems are hypothesized to operate near criticality, enhancing their capacity for optimal information processing, transmission and storage capabilities. Criticality has typically been studied in spiking neural networks and related systems organized in random or full connectivity, with the balance of excitation and inhibition being a key determinant of the critical point of the system. However, given that neurons in the brain are spatially distributed, with their distances significantly influencing connectivity and signal timing, it is unclear how the spatial organization of excitatory and inhibitory connectivity influences the network’s development towards criticality. Here, we systematically constrain the distance and density of inhibitory connectivity in two-dimensional spiking networks and allow synaptic weights to develop with activity-dependent excitatory and inhibitory plasticity in the presence of a low level of stochastic intrinsic activity. We then investigate the relationship between inhibitory connectivity, synaptic weights, and the resulting network activity during and after development. We find that networks with longer-range inhibitory synapses tend towards more supercritical behavior compared to networks with a similar number of shorter-range inhibitory synapses. We show that this distance dependence is a consequence of weaker long-range synapses after development due to the presence of synaptic delays, which shift most spike pairs outside of the potentiation window of the inhibitory learning rule.

abstract.title: Author summary
abstract.p: The brain is thought to operate near a critical state, a regime that supports efficient information processing, transmission, and storage. While previous studies have shown that the balance between excitation and inhibition is important for maintaining criticality, much less is known about how the spatial organization of neural circuits contributes to this process. Using a spatially embedded spiking neural network with biologically motivated synaptic plasticity, we investigated how the range of inhibitory connections influences the development of critical dynamics. We found that networks with predominantly long-range inhibitory connections consistently developed more supercritical activity than networks with similar numbers of short-range inhibitory connections. This effect arose because axonal conduction delays shifted spike timing outside the potentiation window of inhibitory spike-timing-dependent plasticity, preventing distant inhibitory synapses from strengthening effectively. As a result, long-range inhibition provided weaker functional control of network activity despite identical structural connectivity. Our findings identify transmission delays as an important developmental factor linking the spatial organization of inhibitory circuits to network criticality. They further suggest that developmental alterations in inhibitory connectivity may influence brain dynamics by changing the effectiveness of inhibitory interactions, providing experimentally testable predictions for studies of cortical development and neurodevelopmental disorders.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The brain criticality hypothesis states that neurons in the brain are organized in such a way that their collective activity lies at or near the phase transition between ordered and random activity [1,2]. At this critical point, neural activity is characterized by self-similarity and scale-free activity patterns. Criticality in neural networks has been shown to be beneficial in many ways. Criticality leads to optimal computational capacities [3,4] and optimal information transmission [5,6]. Networks operating at or near criticality exhibit high information storage capacity [6–8] and achieve their maximum dynamic range, making them highly sensitive to changes in external stimulation [9,10].

Criticality was first discussed in the field of physics with the sandpile model. There, avalanche event sizes are scale-free, meaning that there is a power-law relationship between the size of avalanches and their frequency or probability of occurrence. Scale-free neural activity, so-called neuronal avalanches, were subsequently discovered in cortical neurons as a signature of criticality [5]. Neuronal avalanches have been observed in various in-vitro and in-vivo experimental models [5,11,12].

How the brain develops into the critical state is an active research question [12–14]. Previous research has revealed that network structure, long-term synaptic plasticity rules, and homeostatic mechanisms can drive networks to develop into a critical state [15–18]. Meanwhile, short-term plasticity is known to expand the critical regime from a finely balanced point to a broad region in parameter space [15,19]. Finally, regardless of how criticality is established, the single most important parameter for its maintenance is the balance of excitation and inhibition (E/I balance) within a network [20–22].

Most research into criticality has been conducted in randomly or fully connected networks, ignoring the spatial dimensionality of the brain and the resulting structural anisotropies. The effect of spatial constraints has been investigated in the context of excitatory connectivity [20,23], while synaptic delays have been shown to affect how quickly networks settle into a steady state [24]. However, to our knowledge, there has been no work investigating the impact of inhibitory connectivity or of the influence of conduction delays on the steady-state activity itself.

Here, we investigate the effect of spatial constraints in inhibitory connectivity on the long-term development of criticality, marking a first foray into a more comprehensive treatment of criticality in networks with spatial dimensions. In addition, unlike related studies using spatial constraints for connectivity only [20,23,25], we explicitly model the delays imposed by conduction along axons and find that such delays have a profound effect on the development of synaptic weights.

sec.title: Network structure
sec.p: We investigated networks of nexc=80 excitatory and ninh=20 inhibitory neurons scattered randomly across a two-dimensional disk with a radius of 2 mm. Network structure was established based on the spatial proximity of neurons, as illustrated in Fig 2A. Specifically, for a given presynaptic neuron of type k∈{exc,inh}, all neurons located within a radius of rk were considered potential postsynaptic targets. From among this subset, synaptic connections were established at random with a uniform probability pk. While excitatory connectivity was fixed at rexc=1.3 mm and pexc=0.6, we varied inhibitory connectivity systematically, with rinh∈{0.5,1,2,3,4} mm and pinh∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,1}, yielding a 5-by-5 grid of parameter settings to explore.

Specifically, spatial positions and excitatory connections were maintained across parameter settings, while the inhibitory connections were constructed in an additive fashion with increasing rinh and pinh. To achieve this, we initialized a scaffold Jinhs∈[0,1](nexc+ninh)×ninh of the adjacency matrix Jinh with a single set of pseudo-random numbers for all 25 parameter settings. The principle of this approach is illustrated with a toy example with eight neurons in Fig 2. We use the term “network prototype” to refer to a single set of 25 networks created in this way, each sharing in common the neuron locations, excitatory connectivity, and parts of inhibitory connectivity. sec.title: Development
sec.p: While the structure of the networks, i.e., the presence or absence of synapses, was fixed, we initialized all synaptic weights to zero to imitate an immature neuronal network or silent synapses [31]. We then simulated each network for 15 hours, allowing weights to develop according to the plasticity rules outlined above. To account for the influence of stochasticity in intrinsic neuronal activity, each simulation was repeated five times with different random seeds.

sec.title: Criticality
sec.p: To investigate criticality properties of the developing networks, we analyzed the neural avalanches and calculated the criticality variable Δp as follows. First, we counted spikes across the network in bins of 1 ms duration. Contiguous periods of non-zero spike counts were defined as “avalanches,” with size S corresponding to the total number of spikes and duration T corresponding to the total length of contiguous bins. Within temporal windows of 5 minutes, we calculated the probability p(s) of observing an avalanche of a given size and approximated the resulting distribution with a power-law function, p(S)=aS−α, using linear least-squares fitting in log–log space (i.e., fitting between log(S) and log(p(S))). Because the avalanche size distribution is approximately linear in the small-size region, we restricted the fitting range to S≤Smax=10. This approach was adapted from [32], in which both the small- and large-size tails were excluded from fitting because of their nonlinearity. In our case, only the large-size tail was excluded, as the small-size region remained approximately linear. To assess the robustness of this choice, we also performed sensitivity analyses using Smax=5,20, confirming that the conclusions obtained with Smax=10were not dependent on the specific fitting range selected.
Finally, the desired measure Δp was defined as the average deviation of the data from this fit across all avalanche sizes, i.e.,

In addition to Δp, we calculated κ, the deviation from a theoretical avalanche size distribution with an exponent b of -1.5, which corresponds to the scaling relation found in living networks [10,20].

As an alternative measure of criticality, we examined the relationships between scaling exponents. In addition to fitting the avalanche size distribution p(S)~S−α, we fitted the lifetime distribution p(T)~T−τ by performing a linear regression on log(T) versus log(p(T)) for T≤Tmax=10. We also analyzed the avalanche size conditioned on lifetime, S(T)~T1/σνz, by linearly fitting log(S(T)) against log(T). Using these fitted exponents, we computed the scaling relation
In systems at criticality, this relation is expected to hold exactly, such that γ=0 [33,34].

We also evaluated the Fano factorF(T)=⟨N2(t,t+T)⟩−⟨N(t,t+T)⟩2⟨N(t,t+T)⟩where N(t,t+T) corresponds to the number of spikes fired across the network in the time between t and t+T. In critical processes, F(T) follows a power law [12].

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our results are presented as follows. First, we will briefly cover the development of the networks over 15 hours of simulation time, giving an intuition for the steady-state activity patterns and their emergence. Then, we will focus on the steady state, comparing activity patterns across different parameter settings and confirming that our outcomes broadly agree with previous findings on the boundary conditions for criticality. Finally, we will investigate how the spatial constraint on inhibitory connections affects criticality, showing that networks with more long-range inhibitory connections tend to be more supercritical than networks with more short-range connections, since long-range inhibitory synapses are weaker than short-range synapses and therefore less able to counter excitatory influence.

sec.title: Development
sec.p: Starting from an initial state with connections established but ineffective (w = 0), networks followed a largely conserved trajectory of changes in weights and activity irrespective of the constraints on inhibitory connectivity. Fig 3 shows an example, elaborated below, of this trajectory in three networks. Other runs (i.e., simulations of the same network with different random seeds for intrinsic activity) and other networks and network prototypes followed a qualitatively very similar profile.

sec.p: Initial activity was sparse, uncoordinated, and driven exclusively by intrinsic voltage fluctuations (Fig 3A and 3B). After four to five hours, excitatory weights (Fig 3C) had grown sufficiently strong to cause coordinated activity, which quickly escalated to highly synchronized network-wide bursting (Fig 3B, middle row). This, in turn, drove inhibitory weights to catch up, providing a degree of counterbalance and allowing networks to control activity into an approximately steady state within one to two hours (Fig 3B, right row). Both firing rate and weights then remained approximately constant until the end of the 15-hour simulation period.

sec.title: Criticality after development
sec.p: To assess the activity patterns at steady state, we focused on the final two hours of simulation (13–15 h) in each network and run. Fig 4A shows raster plots of one network prototype, taken from the final 20 seconds in each of the 25 settings of rinh and pinh. In Fig 4B, we illustrate the derivation of the criticality measure Δp on data from three of these networks, exhibiting supercritical behavior (left, rinh=0.5 mm and pinh=0.1, notice the large number of large avalanches), approximately critical behavior (center, rinh=2 mm and pinh=0.5), and subcritical behavior (right, rinh=4 mm and pinh=1, with few large avalanches).

sec.p: The average values of Δp in the final two hours for each of the 25 parameter configurations are shown individually in Fig 4C. The means of Δp across runs in two sample networks, indicative of the expected outcome for each setting of rinh and pinh, are shown in Fig 4D. We observed supercritical behavior throughout most of the parameter space, being the majority outcome in nearly all conditions, except where inhibitory connectivity was very dense with rinh≥2 mm and pinh=1. Criticality, which we define as |Δp|<0.1, was seen to emerge infrequently in most parameter settings, but it occurred more frequently at high inhibitory connectivity densities. A similar picture emerged from the analysis of κ, which measures the deviation of the avalanche size distribution from a theoretical distribution with exponent -1.5 (see S1 Fig). This measure likewise showed more subcritical outcomes in the upper right quadrant than in other regions of the rinh-pinh space. In sum, the higher the density of inhibitory connections at the outset, the lower the value of Δp became after development.

To assess whether our use of Δp is appropriate, we independently calculated the criticality relation γ=|τ−1α−1−1σνz|, which tends towards 0 for critical networks (see S1 Fig). As shown in Fig 4E, the Δp-γplot shows a minimum around Δp=0, indicating that the two measures largely agree about the extent of criticality in our setup.

Furthermore, we plotted Fano factors in Fig 4F and 4G. Fano factor plots suggests network states close to criticality throughout the parameter space, but only at very short time scales, with levels of activity clustering lower than expected from critical systems at time scales above 30–40 ms.

In the power-law fitting used to calculate Δp, we introduced upper bounds on the fitting range: avalanche size S≤Smax=10and duration T≤Tmax=10. To assess the sensitivity of Δp to these fitting ranges, we repeated the fitting with Smax=Tmax=5or 20. As shown in S2 Fig, both the Δp distribution and the Δp–γ relationship are qualitatively preserved, indicating that our analysis is robust to the choice of Smax and Tmax.

In the following, we will analyze how the spatial constraint imposed on our networks leads to this outcome in the developed state. First, we will confirm that the level of criticality is related to synaptic weight balance, as numerous studies have found (Fig 5). Then, we will take a closer look at the relationship between the spatial constraint – and in particular, the length of inhibitory connections – and the criticality level (Fig 6). Finally, in Figs 7 and 8, we will observe how inhibitory connection length relates to weight balance, leading to a detailed explanation of how greater inhibitory connection length leads to higher levels of Δp.

sec.title: Excitation-inhibition balance in the developed state
sec.p: That higher inhibitory density leads to lower Δp, as shown above, is not prima facie surprising: Previous work [20] has shown that criticality typically emerges when excitation and inhibition hold each other in balance. This is hinted at in the results presented above, where we have used the initial constraint. To verify the role of E/I balance in maintaining criticality in our model, we analyzed the steady state of the networks following development. After development, most synapses of all types had weight values approaching either 0 or 1 (S3 Fig, the fraction of weights within 0.1≤W≤0.9 is less than 5% in almost all networks). Therefore, we set a weight threshold of 0.5, considering any synapses at or above the threshold as active, and any below as inactive. Then, we counted the number of active excitatory and inhibitory synapses onto each neuron (the effective in-degree keff) and averaged across neurons. Plotting the inhibitory against the excitatory effective degree of all 1250 networks (25 parameter settings, 10 networks, 5 runs), we see a clear linear separation between supercritical networks, whose inhibitory effective degree is low, and subcritical networks, whose inhibitory effective degree is high relative to their excitatory effective degree (Fig 5A). The same is true when considering the sum of excitatory and inhibitory weights per neuron rather than the effective degree (Fig 5B). Extracting just the critical networks (|Δp|<0.1, Fig 5C), we find that a linear relationship fits the data well, with Winh=4.10Wexc−12.76 and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.288 (p = 0.0122, n = 179 critical networks). This linear relationship holds across a range of |Δp| cutoff values (S4 Fig). Finally, to describe the relationship between the E/I balance and the criticality indicator Δp across all networks, we regressed Δp against the logarithm of the weight ratio Wexcitbf/Winh (Fig 5D), yielding a significant positive relationship (r = 0.679, p = 4.8e-170, n = 1250). This indicates that, as expected, larger E/I ratios are seen in networks with more supercritical outcomes, and confirms that our model is well-behaved with regards to the emergence (or otherwise) of criticality.

sec.title: Effect of spatial constraint
sec.p: Unlike most previous research, our approach to manipulating networks not only affects connection density or weight, but also network topology based on the spatial relationships between neurons. That is, we wanted to know how the length of inhibitory connections affects criticality independently of connection density. However, the parameters we chose to manipulate the networks, rinh and pinh, both affect connection density. Therefore, to cleanly separate the effects of connection length from those of connection density, we calculated the average inhibitory in-degree and the average inhibitory connection length for each network, sliced the resulting space into bins of roughly equal inhibitory degree, and analyzed the effect of connection length separately in each slice as detailed below. Note that, unlike in the above analysis on E/I balance, here we used the connection blueprint, i.e., all existing connections regardless of their weight after development, to quantify the structurally defined connectivity and thereby capture the effect of the initial constraint.

sec.title: Long-range inhibitory networks yield larger avalanches
sec.p: First, we mapped all networks into the space of mean inhibitory degree kinh (Fig 6A) and mean inhibitory connection length linh (Fig 6B). There is clear clustering of networks, an artifact of the discrete set of parameter values. Plotting linh against kinh (Fig 6C), we also see an obvious absence of any networks in the lower right half of the plot (high degree with short average length) due to the spatial nature of our model. Considering the dynamics, we see that networks with greater kinh clearly show lower Δp (Pearson’s r = -0.62, p = 6e-136, n = 1250; Fig 6A), corroborating the above findings on E/I balance even when ineffective connections are included.

The relationship between Δp and linh is similar, but weaker (r = -0.4, p = 2e-48, n = 1250). Noting the dependence between degree and connection length (Fig 6C; networks with high degree necessarily have many long-range connections), we sought to isolate the influence of connection length linh. To do so, we sliced the data into overlapping bins of width 10 along the kinh axis with bin centers at kinh=5,10,15,…,90,95 (see S5 Fig), such that each slice contained networks of approximately equal degree but potentially very different connection lengths. We then correlated linh in these slices with Δp (see an example in Fig 6D). Surprisingly, and contrary to the relationship in the whole data (Fig 6B), we see that greater linh in fact predicts greater Δp across all slices that include networks from multiple r/p settings (Figs 6E and S5; fitted slopes are greater than 0 as assessed by a one-sided t-test, t = 4.66, p = 2e-4, n = 13). In other words, networks with longer inhibitory connections are more supercritical than networks with a similar number of shorter inhibitory connections.

We note that the slice-wise positive correlations do not conflict with the overall negative correlation (Fig 6B), but rather show that the overall correlation result is largely due to the confound between linh and kinh. In addition, as we show in Figs 6F and S6, the correlation between linh and Δp in slices is not mediated by variations in kinh within the slices, which are not related to linh in a systematic manner (fitted slopes are not significantly different from zero as assessed by a two-sided t-test, t = 1.29, p = 0.22, n = 13).

sec.title: Long-range inhibitory connections are less functional
sec.p: Next, we focused on possible reasons for this relationship. The mediating factor between initial connectivity and critical dynamics after development is, of course, synaptic weight. We analyzed the relationship between average inhibitory (Fig 7A) and excitatory (Fig 7B) weights and the mean length of inhibitory connections linh, controlling for degree as before. We find that longer connections, i.e., higher linh, consistently led to lower inhibitory weight averages, while excitatory weights were unaffected. Put differently, networks with longer-range inhibitory connections developed higher E/I ratios, leading to the more supercritical outcomes observed above.

Why do networks with longer inhibitory connections have lower inhibitory weights? To answer this, we turned to an analysis of individual synaptic weights within networks, correlating inhibitory synaptic weight against the distance between pre- and postsynaptic neurons. As shown in the example in Fig 7C, longer-range inhibitory synapses tend to be weaker than short-range synapses. This holds true across networks in most of the parameter space of rinh and pinh (Fig 7D, top), with an average correlation coefficient of r=−0.32±0.18. The effect is naturally weaker where rinh is so small that there are few inhibitory connections and little variation in their distance to begin with, but very consistent in networks with rinh≥2 mm (Fig 7D, bottom), where the correlation is very strong on average (r=−0.43±0.18).

A small caveat is warranted here. Due to our choice of a hard-bounds STDP rule, weights developed into a bimodal distribution with values of either nearly 0 or nearly 1 as noted above and shown in S3 Fig (the fraction of weights within 0.1≤W≤0.9 is less than 5% in almost all networks). Consequently, the observed lower inhibitory weight average for networks with more long-range connections (Fig 7A) and the negative correlations between length and weight within networks (Fig 7D) should be interpreted in the sense that longer-range connections are less likely to be potentiated into an active state than short-range ones. Put differently, networks with longer average connection lengths have a smaller pool of functional (short-range) inhibitory synapses, and thus a lower effective inhibitory degree. Together with the finding of relatively tight E/I balance constraints on criticality (Fig 5), this neatly explains the higher values of Δp in longer-range networks (Fig 6C).

sec.title: Long-range synapses experience delayed spike synchrony
sec.p: To understand why long-range connections fail to potentiate over development, we then considered the underlying learning rule, the Mexican hat shaped inhibitory STDP rule, and its driving factor, the coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic spikes. If long-range connections are not being strengthened, it must be the case that there are few coincident spike pairs relative to non-coincident spike pairs. To confirm this and understand how distance affects spike coincidence, we turned to a sample network that reaches criticality (rinh=4 mm, pinh=0.7, shown also in Fig 7). We separated synapses into groups by their distance, then considered all spike pairs with a temporal separation at the synapse of less than 50 ms, plotting their occurrence over developmental time as a heatmap (Fig 8A).

In all synapse groups, the early developmental period was marked by very low levels of coincident activity, consistent with low overall activity and a lack of growth in inhibitory weights (cf. Fig 3). After the transition to criticality at ~4.5 hours, all groups showed greatly increased coincident spiking, though with a clear trend towards more frequent coincident spikes in shorter-range synapses (note the different color scales in Fig 8A). Crucially, while the timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes was approximately synchronous in short-range synapses, long-range synapses showed strong asynchrony, with most spike pairings following a post-before-pre pattern (Δt<0). This is shown more clearly still in the histogram over all time in Fig 8B.

To understand this asynchrony, consider that the timing of spike pairs in the above was measured at the synapse, which was modelled at the location of the postsynaptic neuron. Therefore, the presynaptic spike timing included a distance-dependent conduction delay, while the postsynaptic spike was recorded at the time of its emission without delay. Correcting for this delay, i.e., recording as the Δt of a spike pair the time difference of the emission of spikes at the respective neuron rather than that of their arrival at the synapse, we see that all spike pairs, from the shortest-range to the longest-range synapses, strongly tend towards synchrony on average (Figs 8C and S9). Together with the axonal (i.e., presynaptic) delay and the shape of the inhibitory learning rule, this synchrony in spiking therefore leads to potentiation in short-range synapses, but depression in long-range synapses.

To test whether this relationship between synaptic distance and spike-timing asynchrony generalizes across networks and parameter regimes, we quantified the fraction of spike pairs falling within the potentiation window as a function of synaptic distance for all networks, focusing on the final hour of simulation time. For all inhibitory synapses, the mean absolute spike-timing difference |Δt| and the fraction of spike pairs within the potentiation window (relative to all spike pairs separated by less than 50 ms) were computed. Synapses were then grouped into distance bins across all networks. Spike-timing asynchrony increased with distance (Fig 8D), while, as a consequence, the fraction of potentiating spike pairs decreased monotonically with synaptic distance (Fig 8E). A weighted least squares regression of the latter relationship, with weights proportional to the number of synapses per bin and cluster-robust standard errors at the network level, confirmed a strong negative effect of distance (β = −0.219, 95% CI [−0.222, −0.216], p < 10−16), while controlling for pinh and rinh. These results demonstrate that the reduction in coincident spike timing with distance is a robust, network-level phenomenon.

Consequently, many long-range inhibitory synapses are ineffective with weights close to 0, and therefore, networks with a substantial fraction of long-range inhibitory synapses experience both less inhibition and thus a greater tendency towards supercritical dynamics than networks where those same synapses are concentrated in a smaller radius. Tying this back to our connectivity constraints, we should therefore expect networks with small radius rinh and large connection probability pinh to show fewer large avalanches than corresponding networks with larger rinh and smaller pinh. Looking back at Fig 4C, we see exactly this: Networks with rinh=2 mm and pinh=0.7 (mean kinh=41, mean Δp=0.59) are less supercritical than networks with rinh=3 mm and pinh=0.5 (mean kinh=45, mean Δp=0.66), even though the latter have more inhibitory connections.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this work, we demonstrated that criticality is affected by the distance between inhibitory neurons and their postsynaptic targets, in that long-range inhibitory connections tend to be weaker than short-range connections. Networks with preferentially short-range inhibitory connections are therefore more strongly inhibited, biasing the dynamics towards the subcritical phase. We further showed that synaptic delay is the main cause for the lower weights in long-range synapses, highlighting the role of conduction delays in establishing and maintaining criticality.

While we have explained our findings in terms of effective degree as a result of the strongly bimodal weight distributions observed, related work has employed both hard-bound STDP rules leading to bimodal weight distributions and soft-bound STDP rules leading to more realistic unimodal weight distributions but found no substantial difference in the resulting patterns of activity and criticality [18]. This allows us to speculate that in our case, too, a soft-bound rule would lead to similar outcomes in terms of activity while leading to explanations in terms of graded variations of synaptic weight.

Our model does not demonstrate self-organized criticality, referring to systems that intrinsically evolve towards a critical point, as shown by the narrow band of parameter settings that lead to criticality (if indeed there is any, see below), and consequently the large number of networks with persistently sub- or supercritical dynamics. This stands in contrast to related work, where short-term plasticity [15] or long-term plasticity with high learning rates [18] directly contribute to the establishment and maintenance of criticality in a comparatively broad region of parameter space. With our approach to plasticity, with low learning rates enforcing a scale separation between development and dynamics, we chose to highlight the structural, rather than dynamic, contributions to criticality.

There is a clear connection between our results and cortical connectivity patterns, which are widely known to strongly favor short-range local connections for inhibitory synapses [35]. While this has been attributed in part to a reduction of wiring cost [36,37], our work suggests that short-range connectivity also emerges as a consequence of an interplay between the homeostatic quasi-Hebbian learning rule thought to dominate inhibitory long-term plasticity [29] and the frequent occurrence of neuronal avalanches in near-critical networks. In our model, long-range synapses are not weakened because distant neurons are not acting in synchrony – indeed, on average, they are – but rather because transmission delays hinder the consistent temporal coordination of pre- and postsynaptic events. However, unlike our model, cortex possesses higher-order structure, which may bias activity propagation in ways that allow coordinated firing, and therefore strong inhibitory connectivity, over longer distances along frequently used signaling pathways. More fundamentally, the spatial organization of inhibitory circuits is itself subject to developmental constraints imposed by genetic programs, molecular guidance cues, and activity-dependent maturation processes [38,39]. In this sense, the inhibitory radius in our model may be viewed as an abstract representation of developmental constraints on inhibitory circuit formation.

This interpretation generates a testable hypothesis. If the spatial extent of inhibitory connectivity acts as a developmental constraint on criticality, then genetic or developmental perturbations that alter inhibitory neuron migration, axonal growth, or synaptic targeting should systematically shift network dynamics away from criticality. Specifically, our model predicts that reductions in local inhibitory connectivity, or developmental changes that bias inhibitory connectivity toward longer spatial ranges, should produce more supercritical dynamics due to the reduced efficacy of delayed inhibitory interactions. Conversely, enhanced local inhibitory connectivity should bias networks toward more subcritical dynamics. Such effects may be measurable through changes in avalanche statistics, E/I balance, or related criticality metrics during development. This prediction is particularly relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia, where abnormalities in inhibitory circuit development and E/I balance have been widely reported [40–42].

Related work has shown that higher-order structure in the form of hierarchical modularity is conducive to critical dynamics [43,44]. In some cases, even modularity in only the inhibitory connections is sufficient to promote criticality, while excitatory modularity only plays a secondary role [18]. Relatedly, too many long-range connections of either kind make it difficult for networks to achieve criticality at all [25]. These findings align well with our results, since neural modules or clusters of neurons in close spatial proximity are likely to fire in a coordinated manner, supporting the formation of strong inhibitory synapses. How such modules form in the first place, and what defines their boundaries, however, is outside the scope of our exploration.

A first key limitation of the present model is its relatively small network size. With 100 neurons, our simulations are not suited to establishing scale-free criticality in the thermodynamic sense, and caution is warranted when interpreting avalanche statistics. However, the primary conclusion of this study does not depend on demonstrating asymptotic critical scaling, but rather on identifying systematic shifts in network dynamics across matched configurations. In particular, we show that increasing the spatial range of inhibitory connectivity consistently reduces effective inhibition and biases networks toward more supercritical regimes. This relative comparison is robust across network instances and does not rely on absolute scaling properties. Small-scale spiking networks have been widely used to study mechanisms related to criticality, including models with as few as 32 neurons that nonetheless exhibit signatures of critical dynamics [45], as well as modular network models that emphasize structural determinants of criticality [18]. These studies similarly prioritize mechanistic insight over asymptotic scaling behavior. At the same time, it remains an open question whether the distance-dependent inhibitory effects identified here persist in larger networks or in systems with more complex spatial and modular organization. Future work should therefore test the generality of this mechanism in larger-scale models.

A second key limitation lies in the measures used to gauge criticality in our networks. In the results presented above, we focused on Δp, supplemented with the closely related measure κ, with which we see similar results (S1 Fig). However, both measures rely exclusively on the avalanche size distribution. In recognition of the weakness of these measures, which may easily yield results suggesting criticality where there is, in fact, none, we provide a closer analysis of the critical behavior of our networks in S1 and S9 Figs. Our analysis of Fano factors (Fig 4F and 4G) suggests network states close to criticality throughout the parameter space, but only at very short time scales. In the domain of spike avalanches, we also calculated the scaling exponent relation |τ−1α−1−1σνz| [33,34], a test which many of our networks fail (S1 Fig). Note, however, that this criticality relationship varies with Δpas expected (Fig 4E) and shows a similar trend across the space of rinh and pinh, indicating that these measures broadly agree. Further, we note that our results do not depend on true criticality emerging: Rather, the trend towards less supercritical (or more subcritical, or simply more ordered) behavior with greater inhibitory density, but crucially also with longer inhibitory connections, holds in three measures considered (S10 Fig).

Third, we did not evaluate the contribution of short-term depression (STD) to inhibitory connections and criticality. STD has been shown to play a key role in broadening the parameter range for criticality [15,19]. Moreover, STD functions to suppress spurious bursts and activity propagation, thereby preventing supercritical states [26,46]. Although our analysis in Fig 8 suggests that the time window of long-term inhibitory STDP can account for the distance dependence of inhibitory weights, STD may also contribute to this relationship. Understanding how STD and STDP jointly determine criticality will be an important direction for future research.

Whilst we showed that transmission delays have a notable impact on the (effective) structure of a spatially defined network, we have not investigated their dynamical implications. Theoretical considerations have shown that transmission delays affect the time scale of relaxation towards steady state activity when an external input is applied but not the steady state activity itself [24]. In networks of finite size, we suspect that the dynamics may well depend on transmission delays in nontrivial ways and would encourage further research along these lines.

body.p: Reviewer #1: 1. **Substantially strengthen the justification for the specific inhibitory STDP rule.** The "Mexican hat" rule is central to the findings, yet its selection is not sufficiently motivated. You must provide a more rigorous justification for why this specific, non-standard inhibitory STDP rule was chosen over other proposed models (e.g., purely depressive rules). Discuss how its symmetric, Hebbian nature relates to biological findings and explicitly state why its potentiation window is critical for your delay-based hypothesis, as this is the core mechanism of your proposed effect.

2. **Clarify the initial weight initialization protocol and justify the choice of zero weights.** The decision to initialize all synaptic weights to zero is unconventional and requires explicit justification. You must explain how this initial "silent" network state corresponds to a biologically plausible developmental stage (e.g., early postnatal development). Furthermore, detail the exact procedure: are all weights truly zero, or is there a minimal, random initial value to break symmetry? The current description is ambiguous and could significantly impact the initial trajectory of network development.

3. **Provide a rigorous statistical demonstration that the developed weight distributions are indeed bimodal.** The entire argument regarding "effective degree" rests on the claim that weights are bimodal, clustering near 0 and 1. You must supplement Supplementary Figure 3 with quantitative analyses, such as Hartigan's dip test for unimodality or by showing histograms with clear separation. A simple statement that weights "approach either 0 or 1" is not sufficient evidence for such a foundational claim.

4. **Explicitly define and justify the threshold for "criticality" (|Δp| < 0.1).** The choice of this specific threshold is arbitrary and lacks justification. You must provide a statistical or theoretical rationale for this cutoff. Explain how this value was determined and demonstrate its robustness, for instance, by showing that the main conclusions hold across a range of reasonable thresholds.

5. **Directly address the issue of small network size as a potential confound for criticality analysis.** The 100-neuron network is exceptionally small for reliable criticality analysis. You must explicitly discuss how finite-size effects could influence the observed power laws and the Δp metric. Perform and present a finite-size scaling analysis, or at the very least, provide a robust discussion of how your conclusions might be limited by network size and why this model was necessary despite this limitation.

6. **Strengthen the evidence for criticality beyond the avalanche size distribution.** The over-reliance on Δp and κ, both derived from the avalanche size distribution, is a major weakness. You must demonstrate that the "critical" networks also satisfy other hallmarks of criticality. The scaling relation (|(τ-1)/(α-1) - 1/σνz|) should be shown to be near zero for your critical networks, not just correlated with Δp. Furthermore, the Fano factor analysis should be presented in the main text to show a power-law scaling over a substantial range of time windows, not just at "very short time scales."

7. **Quantify the relationship between delay and spike-timing asynchrony more rigorously.** The evidence in Figure 8, while illustrative, is qualitative. You must provide a quantitative analysis across all networks. For instance, plot the mean |Δt| or the fraction of spike pairs within the potentiation window as a function of synaptic distance. This will statistically solidify the claim that delay is the primary cause of the observed asynchrony.

8. **Clarify the analysis of "slices" in Figure 6 and ensure it is not circular.** The method of slicing by kinh to isolate the effect of linh needs a more precise description. Specify the exact binning algorithm (e.g., bin centers, overlaps) and the number of data points in each slice. Ensure that the analysis is not circular, as both kinh and linh are derived from the same underlying connectivity parameters (r_inh, p_inh). The analysis must convincingly demonstrate that the effect of linh is independent of the residual variance in kinh within each slice.

9. **Reconcile the statement that the model does not demonstrate "self-organized criticality" with the manuscript's title and narrative.** You explicitly state that the model does not demonstrate self-organized criticality (SOC) due to the narrow parameter range for criticality. This directly contradicts the title and the narrative of the paper, which focuses on "dynamical development." You must either reframe the manuscript's claims to avoid the term SOC or provide a compelling argument for why this still constitutes a form of self-organization, perhaps by focusing on the weight self-organization towards a balance dictated by spatial constraints.

10. **Discuss the potential interaction between short-term depression (STD) and the observed phenomena.** The model includes STD, a known regulator of criticality. You must discuss what role, if any, STD plays in your results. Is the observed distance-dependence of inhibitory weights robust to the removal of STD? A minimal analysis or a thorough discussion of its potential confounding effects is necessary to isolate the effect of delays and long-term plasticity.

11. **Improve the clarity and interpretability of several key figures.** Figures 4C, 6C, and 7D, which use circular glyphs and complex color-coding, are difficult to interpret. You must redesign these figures for immediate clarity. Consider using standard scatter plots with error bars or panel arrangements that more intuitively represent the data and the statistical distributions. The reader should not have to spend excessive time deciphering the visualization.

12. **Formulate a more precise and testable hypothesis regarding the link to biological cortex in the discussion.** The discussion currently makes a speculative link to biological inhibitory connectivity. Strengthen this by formulating a specific, testable prediction derived from your model. For example, predict that in cortical circuits, the functional weight of inhibitory synapses should decrease with physical distance, even when controlling for other factors, and propose an experimental method (e.g., paired recordings) to test this prediction.

Reviewer #2: In this manuscript, the authors study how constraints on spatial distribution of inhibitory cells in a network of spiking neurons influences its ability to self-organize to criticality. The work is generally well presented and the idea is of interest for the critical brain dynamics community. I have mostly minor comments and one important major revision that could potentially alter interpretation of some results:
Major: Criticality measurements

Criticality measurements are questionable (deviation of data size distribution from power law fit, and deviation from -1.5 power law; also the authors evaluated Fano factor, but the results are only very briefly mentioned in the Discussion and presented on Supp Fig. 2).

1) Great caution needs to be exercised when fitting the avalanche size distributions, specially when one is trying to quantify distance from criticality based on them. I would strongly suggest to perform the fit on log space (fit a linear function to the log of frequency vs the log of sizes). Also, maximum likelihood fitting might be more appropriate. Finally, the cutoff for the distributions must be taken into account and removed from the power law fitting. Results could change qualitatively after a more precise method is employed.

2) Finally, the deviation from criticality measure employed (known as DCC in the literature) in Fig. 4E has been shown to give inconsistent results (e.g. Srinivasan et al. 2024), so interpretation must be done carefully here. For example here in Fig. 4E, one could interpret that based on that measure the negative Dp (which the authors interpret as subcritical) is as closer to criticality than the close to zero Dp.
Minor:
3) Intro needs work. Some concepts are not explained well (e.g. avalanches on sandpile model are not "triggered in a scale-free manner").
4) External drive or "noise" perhaps too high (0.28 Hz intrinsic firing)? What happens if a (order(s) of magnitude) lower value is used?
5) In development examples (Fig. 3), it might be good to add examples of sub, crit and supercritical network development.
6) Fig. 4: avalanche size distributions need to be log-binned for proper evaluation of cut-offs; this would help distinguish slightly subcritical from critical cases.

7) In Fig. 5B-D, when calculating total weight, is the weight threshold in place? It wasn't clear to me. If so, I would suggest removing it from this analyses, since a great number of weak connections could be as effective in driving a cell as a few strong ones.
8) Include subtitles above Fig. 8B and C to more readily distinguish what is being shown.

Reviewer #2: Thanks for thoroughly addressing all my remarks. I do have one final comment that I strongly suggest to address before publication. In your revision, you included a comment in the Discussion on the exponent obtained from the size distribution analysis (~2, instead of the expected 1.5 from branching theory). First, I'd like to emphasize that the 1.5 value in the context of a directed percolation universality class is only expected in high-dimensional systems (d = 4+), such as a random network (Munoz et al., PRE 1999). Your simulation is of a 2D network (directed percolation exponent of ~1.3), although given its small size compared to connection range, it is hard to predict where it would fall exponent-wise. The paper you compare your results to (Yang et al., PRL 2025) employs a random network. Furthermore, and more importantly, avalanche size exponents are *known* to vary with binning (a serious limitation of the method, hence my scrutiny in the initial revision with the methods chosen for criticality evaluation - see e.g., Capek et al., Nat Commun 2023), rendering the discussion of possible deviations from expected exponents fruitless. I therefore strongly suggest to either remove the exponent remark or at the very least include this caveat on the publication.
